acts.title: Living on the water
text: Marina Kovacs has lived on the same boat for eleven years. It is moored on a canal about forty minutes from the centre of Amsterdam, and it is the only permanent home she has ever owned.
“People always ask the same two questions,” she says. “Is it cold, and what are you going to do when you’re old? It isn’t cold. And I don’t know yet.”

Life on the water has rules that people on the mainland never think about. On some stretches of the canal you have to move the boat every fourteen days. You aren’t allowed to run the engine after ten at night. The shower is a cubicle roughly the size of a phone box, and the washing machine is communal — three families share it, and you have to book a slot.
The compensations, she says, are obvious the moment you wake up. “In the summer I set off at six and I’m at work in the city by seven. In February I don’t move for a month.”

She is not alone. There are now thousands of floating homes in the Netherlands, and several cities are planning whole floating districts. Architects predict that by 2050 the number will rise sharply, because the alternative — building inland, further and further from work — is running out of space. “I think it’ll become completely normal,” Marina says. “People said the same about the suburbs a hundred years ago.”
So is she going to stay? “I’ve decided to keep the boat for now. I’ll probably buy something on land eventually, when I want a garden. But I’ll never feel at home in a building that can’t move.”

tts: Yesterday we took the train from La Paz into Peru, and today we’re going to visit the floating islands on Lake Titicaca.
Ever since I first heard about these islands in a geography class, I’ve wanted to see them.
I don’t really enjoy boat trips, but I’m sure the water will be quite calm, as it’s a clear sunny day.
It’s quite cold, though, so I’m going to take an extra sweater to keep warm.
I believe we’ll be able to ask the inhabitants questions through a guide.
I’d also like to know what they think the future holds. Do they think their children will stay on the islands?
It would be great to have some photos for the blog, so I’ll take my camera too.

o: Take the train to La Paz

items.q: Why is she taking an extra sweater?
o: Because the boat has no roof

items.q: What does she decide as she is speaking?
o: To take her camera as well

write.q: Write about where you live now and where you expect to be in ten years. Use be going to for a decision you have already made, will for a prediction, and will probably or probably won’t for something you are less sure about.
plan: what you are less sure about
write.model: At the moment I live in a flat on the ninth floor, about twenty minutes from the centre. I’ve decided to stay here for at least another year, because the rent is reasonable and I can walk to work. After that I’m going to look for somewhere with a small garden — my sister has already promised to help me look. I think this part of the city will change a lot in the next ten years: three new blocks are going up on the same street. I’ll probably still be here in five years. In ten, though, I probably won’t. I’d like to live somewhere I can see the peaks from the window.

speak.q: Talk for about a minute: what are you definitely going to do this year, and what do you think will happen to your city in ten years? Make the difference between the decision and the prediction clear.
speak.model: This year I’m going to move — I’ve decided already, and I’ve told the landlord. I’m going to look for somewhere with a garden. As for the city, I think it’ll change a lot. Three new blocks are going up on my street alone. I’ll probably still be living here in five years, but in ten I probably won’t.
